title: TCP three-way handshake
summary: A client opens a TCP connection to a server on port 443. The first SYN is lost and retransmitted, then both ends exchange initial sequence numbers and reach ESTABLISHED.

steps.label: passive OPEN
steps.title: The server starts listening on port 443
steps.desc: A program on the server asks TCP to accept connections on port 443. This is a passive OPEN: nothing is sent. The server just waits in the LISTEN state.
notes: No connection exists yet, so there are no sequence numbers on either side.

steps.label: active OPEN, ISS = 1000
steps.title: The client picks an initial sequence number
steps.desc: A program on the client asks TCP to connect (an active OPEN). TCP creates a connection record and picks an initial send sequence number (ISS). This example uses 1000 so the arithmetic is easy to follow.

notes: A real ISS is a 32-bit number that is hard to guess: a clock value plus a keyed hash of the two addresses and ports (RFC 6528). Guessable numbers would let an outsider inject data.

steps.label: SYN seq=1000
steps.title: First SYN is lost on the way
steps.desc: The client sends a SYN carrying its ISS and enters SYN-SENT. This copy is dropped somewhere in the network. TCP is built on a network that may lose packets, so this is a normal event, not an error.
steps.fail: A router on the path dropped the packet. Nothing tells the client: the only sign is that no reply comes back.

notes: The SYN flag takes up one sequence number even though it carries no data. That is why SND.NXT is now 1001.

steps.label: timer expires after 1 s
steps.title: The retransmission timer runs out
steps.desc: When the client sent the SYN it started a retransmission timer. No round-trip time has been measured yet, so the timeout starts at 1 second. It expires with no reply, so the client sends the same SYN again and doubles the timeout.
notes: The 1 second starting value and the doubling come from RFC 6298.
A client does not retry for ever. Linux, for example, retransmits a SYN 6 times by default (tcp_syn_retries) before reporting a timeout to the program.

steps.label: SYN seq=1000 (again)
steps.title: The retransmitted SYN arrives
steps.desc: The second copy is identical to the first: same ports, same sequence number. The SYN also carries options that can only be agreed during the handshake, such as the largest segment the client can receive (MSS).

rows: Number of the first byte this segment occupies in the sender's stream.
How many bytes the sender of this segment is willing to receive.

notes: MSS 1460 = a 1500-byte Ethernet payload minus 20 bytes of IPv4 header and 20 bytes of TCP header.

steps.label: record 1000, ISS = 5000
steps.title: The server records the client's number and picks its own
steps.desc: The SYN matches a listening port. The server creates its own connection record, stores the client's initial sequence number (IRS = 1000), expects byte 1001 next, and picks its own ISS, 5000 in this example.

notes: If nothing were listening on port 443, the server would answer with a RST segment and the client would report "connection refused".

steps.label: SYN, ACK seq=5000 ack=1001
steps.title: The server answers with SYN, ACK
steps.desc: One segment does two jobs. The ACK flag with acknowledgment 1001 says "I received your SYN and expect byte 1001 next". The SYN flag with sequence 5000 says "my own numbering starts here".

steps.label: is ack 1001 acceptable?
steps.title: The client checks the acknowledgment
steps.desc: The client accepts the segment only if it acknowledges something the client really sent: SND.UNA < ack <= SND.NXT, here 1000 < 1001 <= 1001. It passes, so the client records the server's number (IRS = 5000) and moves to ESTABLISHED.

notes: A SYN, ACK with a wrong acknowledgment number (an old duplicate, or a forgery) is answered with a RST instead.

steps.label: ACK seq=1001 ack=5001
steps.title: The client acknowledges the server's SYN
steps.desc: The third segment acknowledges the server's SYN: acknowledgment 5001 means "I expect byte 5001 next". It carries no SYN flag and no data, so it does not use up a sequence number.

rows: Number of the first byte this segment occupies in the sender's stream.
The next byte this side expects from the other.
How many bytes the sender of this segment is willing to receive.

notes: From the client's point of view the connection is already open. It may send data straight after this segment, or even inside it.

steps.label: is ack 5001 acceptable?
steps.title: The server checks the acknowledgment and is connected
steps.desc: The server runs the same test on its side: 5000 < 5001 <= 5001. It passes, so the server moves to ESTABLISHED. Both ends now know both starting numbers, and each has proof the other received its own.

notes: This is why the handshake needs three segments: each side must send its number and see it acknowledged, and the middle segment combines one acknowledgment with one number.

steps.label: PSH, ACK seq=1001 len=517
steps.title: First data: the sequence numbers start counting bytes
steps.desc: The client sends 517 bytes (here a TLS ClientHello, since this is port 443). The segment starts at sequence 1001, the number after the SYN. The server will acknowledge 1001 + 517 = 1518.

simplifications: Sequence numbers start at 1000 and 5000 for readability. Real initial sequence numbers are 32-bit values chosen to be hard to guess.
Only one loss is shown. Real stacks keep retransmitting with a growing timeout and give up after a limit set by the operating system.
The IP header is reduced to three fields, and link-layer framing, routing hops and NAT are left out.
Options are listed but not explained in depth: window scaling, selective acknowledgment and timestamps each have their own rules.
SYN flood defences (SYN cookies, backlog limits), simultaneous open and TCP Fast Open are not covered.
Connection teardown (FIN) is not part of this explainer.
